extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in wartime/current events
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting on military operations, political/diplomatic reactions, and civilian effects during an armed conflict for a general newspaper audience; emphasizes sourcing, verification, and context. The article mixes frontline dispatches, official statements, rumors, and human-interest details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Name and attribute information to its origin (e.g., 'By the Associated Press', 'Reuters intercepted', 'the Belgian Premier said', 'British communiques').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always attribute claims to specific agencies, officials, communiques or broadcasts as in the article (Reuters, Associated Press, official broadcasts, government communiques). Use clear tags like 'reported', 'said', 'a communique said' to show provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rumors from verified facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag material presented as rumor vs confirmed report (examples: 'These rumors said...', 'Most of these reports could not be checked').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear when information is unverified; qualify with phrases such as 'were rumored', 'reported to have', or 'could not be checked'. Avoid treating rumor as fact and include caveats provided by sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report official statements and government positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Give space to formal statements and broadcasts from governments and leaders (e.g., 'Premier Hubert Pierlot told the nation', 'The Swiss Federal Council issued a statement').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include direct or summarized quotations of official pronouncements, note broadcast audiences (heard in London, heard in Brussels), and report governmental actions (mobilization, protests, diplomatic notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide historical and contextual background
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextualize current events with relevant history and background (example: Sedan's role in 1870 and 1914; 'It brought about the fall of the Second Empire.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add concise historical background that illuminates strategic or symbolic importance of places/events to help readers understand stakes and precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic specificity and place naming
rubrics_metrics.description: List precise places, front lines, valleys and distances (e.g., 'Meuse Valley', 'Sedan line lies seven miles within French territory', towns: Liege, Namur, Dinant, Longwy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify locations, directions, and relative distances; name towns, rivers, front sectors and flanks to orient readers geographically and clarify movement of forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-impact / refugee and civilian detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Report civilian effects and refugee movements (examples: 'trains filled with refugees', 'peasants trudged down the roads with carts, livestock and meager furnishings').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include eyewitness or reported descriptions of refugees, civilian casualties, and daily hardships to convey humanitarian consequences, using concrete imagery and numbers where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military detail and equipment description
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe weaponry, vehicles and aircraft with specific performance claims (examples: 'flame-throwing tanks hurled lethal fire seventy yards', descriptions of new fighters/bombers 'Beaufort', 'Defiant', 'power-operated turret').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide technical details and claimed ranges/capabilities but couple them with source attribution or verification status; distinguish official claims from observed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present competing claims and contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report contrasting accounts from opposing sides and note disputes (example: Germany claims capture of Liege while Belgian premier denies forts have fallen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where authorities differ, present both statements and make the contradiction explicit so readers can see uncertainty and competing narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on sensational/extraordinary claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat sensational or extraordinary reports skeptically (example: 'Germany’s new secret weapon... described as a death-dealing wave' but later noted 'in the absence of any official statement' and that it 'was merely the use of parachute troops').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label extraordinary claims, seek corroboration, and when none is available indicate official silence or alternative, more prosaic explanations as the article does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and attribution of intercepted or secondhand communications
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on intercepted radio messages or foreign broadcasts, identify interception source and describe content (examples: 'Reuters intercepted a radio message', 'Rome broadcast intercepted here by the Columbia Broadcasting System').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State that material was intercepted, name the intercepting organization, and note limitations or possible biases associated with such sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil-defense and practical governmental orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Report civic preparedness measures and official civil-defense guidance (examples: 'air-raid alarms sounded', 'Organize Boy Scouts and Women to Spot Foes in Sky', orders to evacuate or assemble internees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey government advice and measures (mobilization, evacuations, civil organization) clearly and precisely so readers understand recommended actions and official steps being taken.
